expectedText:
CALIFORNIA WAREHOUSE QUOTA LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Distribution, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's warehouse quota law, Labor Code §§ 2100–2112 (Part 8.6 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, added by Stats. 2021, Ch. 197 (AB 701), effective January 1, 2022), as it may relate to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme Distribution, Inc. It explains how the statute defines a covered "warehouse distribution center employer" and a "quota," the written quota disclosure the statute requires of a covered employer, the statute's limits on a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods or bathroom use, and the statute's employee data-request and retaliation-presumption provisions. This document does not itself determine whether Acme Distribution, Inc. meets the statute's coverage threshold, and it does not constitute or substitute for the written quota disclosure a covered employer is required to provide.

COVERAGE: WHICH EMPLOYERS AND QUOTAS THE STATUTE REACHES
California's warehouse quota law defines a "quota" as a work standard under which an employee is assigned or required to perform at a specified productivity speed, to perform a quantified number of tasks, or to handle or produce a quantified amount of material, within a defined time period, where the employee may suffer an adverse employment action for failing to meet the standard. The statute applies only to an "employer" that employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of 100 or more employees at a single warehouse distribution center, or 1,000 or more employees at one or more warehouse distribution centers in the state — counting all employees of the employer's commonly controlled group toward that threshold. A "warehouse distribution center" is defined by specific North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes covering general warehousing and storage, and durable- and nondurable-goods merchant wholesalers, and electronic shopping and mail-order houses; the statute expressly excludes the NAICS code for farm product warehousing and storage. Whether Acme Distribution, Inc.'s workplace meets this employee-count and NAICS-code threshold is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "“Employer” means a person who directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person, including through the services of a third-party employer, temporary service, or staffing agency or similar entity, employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of 100 or more employees at a single warehouse distribution center or 1,000 or more employees at one or more warehouse distribution centers in the state."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(f), California Labor Code, definition of "employer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2100.)
  "“Quota” means a work standard under which an employee is assigned or required to perform at a specified productivity speed, or perform a quantified number of tasks, or to handle or produce a quantified amount of material, within a defined time period and under which the employee may suffer an adverse employment action if they fail to complete the performance standard."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(h), California Labor Code, definition of "quota" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2100.)
  "“Warehouse distribution center” means an establishment as defined by any of the following North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Codes, however that establishment is denominated: (A) 493110 for General Warehousing and Storage. (B) 423 for Merchant Wholesalers, Durable Goods. (C) 424 for Merchant Wholesalers, Nondurable Goods. (D) 454110 for Electronic Shopping and Mail-Order Houses."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(i), California Labor Code, definition of "warehouse distribution center" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2100.)
  Known gap: The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2100) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This statute does not apply to every employer that uses a quota system; it applies only to a "warehouse distribution center employer" that both falls within one of the statute's four listed NAICS codes (and is not the excluded farm-product-warehousing code) and meets the 100-employee/single-center or 1,000-employee/statewide threshold, aggregating the employer's commonly controlled group as defined by Revenue and Taxation Code § 25105. The statute separately defines "employee" (§ 2100(d)) as a nonexempt employee who works at a warehouse distribution center — a definition this clause paraphrases but does not quote.

THE WRITTEN QUOTA DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENT
California law requires a covered warehouse distribution center employer to provide each employee, upon hire or within 30 days of the statute's effective date, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject. That written description must include the quantified number of tasks to be performed, or materials to be produced or handled, within the defined time period, and any potential adverse employment action that could result from failing to meet the quota.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Each employer shall provide to each employee, upon hire, or within 30 days of the effective date of this part, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject, including the quantified number of tasks to be performed or materials to be produced or handled, within the defined time period, and any potential adverse employment action that could result from failure to meet the quota."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2101, California Labor Code, the written quota disclosure requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2101.)
  Known gap: This disclosure requirement applies only to an employer that meets the "warehouse distribution center employer" threshold described elsewhere in this document; the statute does not specify a particular form or format for the written description beyond requiring these three categories of content. This clause does not itself constitute or satisfy that written disclosure for any quota the employer applies to the employee.

LIMITS: A QUOTA MAY NOT PREVENT MEAL/REST COMPLIANCE OR BATHROOM USE
California law prohibits requiring an employee to meet a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods, use of bathroom facilities — including reasonable travel time to and from bathroom facilities — or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or Division of Occupational Safety and Health standards. An employer may not take adverse employment action against an employee for failing to meet a quota that does not allow the employee to comply with meal and rest periods or those occupational health and safety laws, or for failing to meet a quota that was not disclosed to the employee as required by § 2101. Separately, time an employee spends complying with occupational health and safety laws counts as time on task and productive time for purposes of any quota or monitoring system, though meal and rest breaks themselves are not counted as productive time unless the employee is required to remain on call.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "An employee shall not be required to meet a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods, use of bathroom facilities, including reasonable travel time to and from bathroom facilities, or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards. An employer shall not take adverse employment action against an employee for failure to meet a quota that does not allow a worker to comply with meal and rest periods, or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards, or for failure to meet a quota that has not been disclosed to the employee pursuant to Section 2101."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2102, California Labor Code, quota limits on meal/rest periods and bathroom use (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2102.)
  "meal and rest breaks are not considered productive time unless the employee is required to remain on call."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2103(b), California Labor Code, meal/rest breaks not counted as productive time (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2103.)
  Known gap: This part of the statute cross-references, rather than restates, California's separate meal- and rest-period requirements and occupational health and safety standards; it does not itself define what makes a particular meal or rest period or bathroom break compliant. The § 2103 citation below addresses a separately numbered section of this same statutory part and is independent of the § 2102 citation — not two subsections of one section.

EMPLOYEE'S RIGHT TO REQUEST QUOTA AND PERSONAL WORK SPEED DATA
If a current or former employee believes that meeting a quota caused a violation of the employee's right to a meal or rest period, or required the employee to violate an occupational health and safety law in the Labor Code or a Division of Occupational Safety and Health standard, California law gives the employee the right to request — and requires the employer to provide — a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject and a copy of the most recent 90 days of the employee's own personal work speed data. A former employee who makes this request receives 90 days of quota and work speed data measured back from the employee's date of separation, and is limited to one such request. An employer that receives a written or oral request under this right must comply as soon as practicable, and no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. The statute does not require an employer to use quotas or monitor work speed data in the first place, and an employer that does not monitor this data has no obligation to produce it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "If a current or former employee believes that meeting a quota caused a violation of their right to a meal or rest period or required them to violate any occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards, they have the right to request, and the employer shall provide, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject and a copy of the most recent 90 days of the employee’s own personal work speed data."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(a)(1), California Labor Code, the employee data request right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2104.)
  "An employer that receives a written or oral request for information pursuant to subdivision (a) shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(b), California Labor Code, the employer's 21-day response deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2104.)
  "Nothing in this section requires an employer to use quotas or monitor work speed data. An employer that does not monitor this data has no obligation to provide it."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(c), California Labor Code, no obligation to monitor or use quotas (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2104.)
  Known gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2104) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This is a conditional right, not a general right to request quota data at any time: it is triggered specifically by the employee's belief that meeting a quota caused a meal- or rest-period violation or required violating an occupational health and safety law, and the statute's own text does not describe a broader, unconditional right to the same information.

THE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION OF RETALIATION
California law creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer in any manner discriminates, retaliates, or takes any adverse action against an employee within 90 days of the employee initiating the employee's first request in a calendar year for quota or personal work speed data information, or of the employee making a complaint related to a quota that alleges a violation of §§ 2101 through 2104 to the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, another local or state governmental agency, or the employer itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "there shall be a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer in any manner discriminates, retaliates, or takes any adverse action against any employee within 90 days of the employee doing either of the following:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2105, California Labor Code, the retaliation presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2105.)
  Known gap: This is a rebuttable presumption, not a conclusive one — the statute's own text does not itself define what evidence rebuts it. The presumption applies only within the 90-day window described above and only to the two triggering acts identified in § 2105(a) and § 2105(b) (a first-in-calendar-year information request, or a complaint alleging a violation of §§ 2101–2104); adverse action taken outside that window, or unconnected to those triggering acts, is not addressed by this presumption.
